title: Why Can't You Move Just ONE Eye? 👀
description:
Move just one eye. Only your left. Go! Can't? Almost nobody can. Your brain doesn't steer your eyes one at a time: every look is ONE order sent to both eyes at once, like two dogs on one leash. Now close one eye, rest a fingertip lightly on the lid and look around: you can feel the shut eye moving too. It's still on the walk, blindfolded.
A chameleon is different: its eyes can scan two ways at once, one forward and one back... until it spots a fly. Then both swing onto it, just before the tongue shoots.
Did only one move? Yes or no?

The science: Hering's law of equal innervation (Ewald Hering, 1868). The matching muscles of your two eyes get the same command, so the eyes move as a pair. You CAN turn them both inward (cross-eyed), but that is another both-eyes command, not one eye on its own. Scientists still argue about the fine print.

Chameleons: Katz et al., Journal of Experimental Biology, 2015. Their eyes scan on their own, then the second eye swings over to the same target before the strike.
